title: Kalimpong Food: Cheese, Momos, Churpi and Village Kitchens
meta_description: What to eat in Kalimpong, Lava and Lolegaon: momos, thukpa, sha phaley, Kalimpong cheese and lollipops, churpi, gundruk and Lepcha home food, with prices.
summary: Eat momos, thukpa and sha phaley in Kalimpong's bazaar, buy Kalimpong cheese and milk lollipops, and try churpi, gundruk, kinema and squash shoots in village homestays. Most meals cost ₹80–300. The food mixes Nepali, Tibetan, Lepcha and Bengali kitchens, which is the history of the town on a plate.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: Kalimpong eats the way it was settled. The Lepcha were here first; Bhutanese, Nepali, Tibetan, Bengali, Marwari and Scottish arrivals followed over three centuries, and each left something in the kitchen. In the bazaar you will eat Tibetan momos, thukpa and sha phaley; in a homestay, Nepali rice, dal and seasonal greens with a sharp pickle; in a Lepcha village, nettle soup, millet and bamboo shoots. And there is the town's own food, born of a Swiss priest's dairy: Kalimpong cheese and milk lollipops.

Eating is cheap. A plate of momos costs ₹60–120, a bowl of thukpa ₹100–180 and a full rice thali with refills ₹150–250. Village homestays include dinner and breakfast in their rate, and those meals are usually the best food of a trip, cooked from the garden that morning. Prices below are indicative for 2025–26.

sections.heading: A Swiss priest's cheese and lollipops
paras: In the 1950s Father André Butty, a Swiss Jesuit who had hoped to work in Tibet, was stopped short of the border and stayed in Kalimpong. To support a mission orphanage, he set up the Swiss Welfare Dairy and taught local workers to make a firm, mild cheese in the style he knew from home, and lollipops of milk boiled down in iron pans until it turned to dark, chewy toffee. The dairy became part of the town's identity. It closed in 1990, when Father Butty's visa was not renewed and he had to leave India.

Kalimpong cheese and lollipops survive with smaller local makers. Ask in grocery and dairy shops in the bazaar and along Main Road, and buy lollipops by the piece or in packets; they make good, light presents. Supplies of cheese are small and vary by season, so buy it when you see it. Keep it cool on the way home, and wrap it well if you are taking it on a long train journey.

sections.heading: Tibetan cafés and the bazaar
paras: Tibetan traders lived in Kalimpong long before 1959, when the wool caravans came down from Lhasa over Jelep La, and refugees settled after the Dalai Lama's flight. Their food is now everyday town food. Small cafés around the Motor Stand, Main Road and the lanes of the bazaar serve momos from breakfast time, thukpa and thenthuk at lunch, and sha phaley, a crisp fried bread packed with spiced meat, as a snack. Ask for the house chilli sauce, which is usually fiery.

Pork momos are the local favourite, but chicken, vegetable and cheese momos are everywhere, and many cafés make a mixed plate. Tingmo, a soft steamed bun, goes with meat curries. In summer, look for laphing, a cold dish of mung-bean jelly noodles in chilli oil and garlic, sold from small stalls. Butter tea, salty and rich, is worth one cup for the experience; most people then return to sweet milk tea.

Not everything in the bazaar is Tibetan. Marwari trading families, who came with the wool trade, run sweet shops and vegetarian eateries where you can eat puri, kachori, samosa and jalebi for breakfast at ₹40–100. Bengali visitors keep a few fish-and-rice places busy in season, and roadside dhabas on the way in serve egg curry, chowmein and rice plates. If you tire of momos after three days, as some people do, a plain vegetarian thali of rice, dal, sabzi and curd is never far away, and it is often the cheapest full meal in town.

Go to the haat on Wednesday or Saturday morning, near the Motor Stand, to see what the hills grow. Villagers lay out squash shoots, ningro fern tips, bamboo shoots, dalle khursani (the small, round, very hot local chilli), dried fish, churpi and seasonal fruit: oranges in winter, plums and pears in summer. Confirm haat days locally.

sections.heading: Homestay kitchens in the villages
paras: In Sillery Gaon, Icchey Gaon, Ramdhura, Kolakham and the other homestay villages, dinner is what the family cooks that day. Expect rice, dal, a seasonal vegetable, a green such as mustard or spinach saag, a pickle and, if you have asked for it, chicken, pork or eggs. Vegetables come from the kitchen garden: iskus (chayote) and its tender shoots, pumpkin leaves, radish, beans and potatoes. Breakfast is often puri and aloo, paratha or bread and eggs.

This is where you meet the fermented foods of the Nepali hills. Gundruk is leafy greens fermented and sun-dried, cooked into a sour soup or pickle. Kinema is soybeans fermented until sticky and strong-smelling, then cooked as a curry. Soft churpi is cooked with chilli and tomato into a hot relish. Ask your host to show you how gundruk is made if you visit in autumn, when the greens are fermented for the year.

Tell your host about any dietary needs when you book, not at dinner time, as villages are far from shops. Vegetarian meals are easy everywhere; vegan meals need explaining, since ghee and milk are common. Meal times are early in the villages: dinner is often served by 7.30 or 8 pm, so that the family can clear up and sleep. Join them in the kitchen if invited; it is usually the warmest room in the house.

sections.heading: Lepcha food in Lolegaon and Charkhole
paras: The Lepcha villages east of Kalimpong, among them Lolegaon and Charkhole, keep a forest-based cooking that rarely appears on restaurant menus. Families gather nettles for soup, cook bamboo shoots fresh and fermented, grow millet and maize, and use wild greens and ferns picked from the forest edge. Meals are simple and seasonal, and the best way to taste them is to ask your homestay host in advance whether they can cook a Lepcha dinner.

Millet beer, called chi by the Lepcha, is brewed in many hill homes and drunk on festival days, at weddings and in welcome. It is usually served warm, from a vessel topped up with hot water and sipped through a bamboo straw. Accept it as hospitality if you drink, sip slowly, and do not feel obliged if you do not. To learn more before you go, visit the Lepcha Museum on the edge of Kalimpong town.

sections.heading: Tea, festival food and what to carry home
paras: Kalimpong is not a big tea district like Darjeeling, but tea is everywhere. Stalls serve sweet milk tea for ₹15–30; better cafés serve Darjeeling and local hill teas. At Dashain and Tihar, in October and November, homes fry sel roti, ring-shaped rice-flour bread, and visitors are often offered it with tea. At Losar, Tibetan families make khapse, fried biscuits in twisted shapes, for guests.

For presents, carry light things that travel well: lollipops, packets of hard churpi, a jar of dalle khursani pickle, dried large cardamom, which is grown on these slopes, and loose tea. Buy cheese last, on your way out of town.
list: Eat in busy places where food turns over fast.
Drink bottled or filtered water; most homestays offer boiled water.
Ask before ordering pork momos if you avoid pork; many cafés use a mixed menu.
Dalle khursani is far hotter than it looks; start with a sliver.

faqs.q: What food is Kalimpong famous for?
faqs.a: Kalimpong is known for its own cheese and milk lollipops, first made at Father André Butty's Swiss Welfare Dairy in the mid-20th century, and for Tibetan momos, thukpa and sha phaley in the bazaar. In homestays, gundruk, kinema, churpi and fresh squash shoots show the Nepali and Lepcha roots of hill food.

faqs.q: Where can I buy Kalimpong cheese?
faqs.a: Ask in grocery and dairy shops in the bazaar and along Main Road. The original Swiss Welfare Dairy closed in 1990, so today's cheese comes from smaller local makers, and supply varies by season. Buy it when you see it, keep it cool and wrap it well for a long journey.

They are sweets made from milk boiled down to a dark, chewy toffee and wrapped around a stick. They were first made at Father André Butty's Swiss Welfare Dairy. Local makers still sell them by the piece or in packets in the bazaar for a few rupees each. They travel well and make good presents.

faqs.q: How much does food cost in Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Momos cost ₹60–120 a plate, thukpa ₹100–180, a full rice thali ₹150–250 and tea ₹15–30 at a stall. A traveller eating in local places spends about ₹400–700 a day. Village homestays include dinner and breakfast in their rate of about ₹1,300–2,200 per person. Prices are indicative for 2025–26.

faqs.q: Is vegetarian food easy to find in Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Yes. Every eatery serves vegetable momos and a vegetarian thali, and homestays cook rice, dal, vegetables and saag daily. Tell homestays about your diet when you book. Vegan travellers should explain that they avoid ghee, milk and butter, which are common in hill cooking.

Churpi is a cheese made from yak or cow milk in the Himalaya. Soft churpi is cooked into curries and hot relishes; hard churpi is dried until stone-hard and chewed slowly for an hour or more. Buy hard churpi at the haat or grocers. Go gently with your teeth.

faqs.q: When is the Kalimpong haat bazaar?
faqs.a: The main haat is held on Wednesdays and Saturdays near the Motor Stand, when villagers bring vegetables, ferns, chillies, churpi, baskets and fruit. Arrive before 10 am for the best of it. Days can shift around festivals and holidays, so confirm locally before you plan around it.

faqs.q: Can I try Lepcha food near Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Yes, mainly in Lepcha homestays in villages such as Lolegaon and Charkhole. Ask your host in advance for a Lepcha dinner: nettle soup, bamboo shoots, millet and forest greens are typical. Restaurants in town rarely serve it. The Lepcha Museum in Kalimpong is a good first stop to learn about the culture.

faqs.q: Is street food in Kalimpong safe?
faqs.a: Generally, if you choose busy stalls where food is cooked fresh in front of you. Momos and thukpa straight from the steamer or pot are a safe bet. Avoid cut fruit and salads that have sat out, drink bottled or filtered water, and take it slowly with the chilli sauces.
